provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of the Bhagavad Gita, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Edwin Arnold 1885; Kashinath Trimbak Telang 1882) and checked against the Sanskrit; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, chapter by chapter.

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders the Bhagavad Gita in plain modern English that keeps the urgency of its battlefield setting and the depth of its teaching — duty and devotion, the deathless self, and acting without grasping at the fruit of action — while shedding the Victorian ornament of the older verse.
introduction: The Gita is a single conversation set at a terrible moment: the warrior Arjuna, about to fight a war against his own kin, lays down his bow and refuses. His charioteer — the god Krishna in disguise — answers him, and the answer becomes the most beloved scripture of India: how to act in the world without being bound by it. Read it as one long dialogue between despair and the divine.

divergences.phrase: from my weak hand slips Gandiv, the goodly bow
divergences.older: from my weak hand slips / Gandiv, the goodly bow (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: Gandiva, my great bow, slips from my hand
divergences.note: The Sanskrit names the bow — Gandiva — and says it is slipping (sramsate) from his hand. Arnold keeps the name but pads the line with "goodly" and "weak hand." We keep the proper noun, which is load-bearing (Gandiva is Arjuna's identity as the supreme archer), and let the plain fact carry the weight: the hero's own weapon is falling out of his grip. The image is the chapter's hinge — the warrior physically unable to hold his bow — and prefigures the closing line where he lets it drop entirely.

divergences.phrase: papam evashrayed asman hatvaitan atatayinah
divergences.older: If they be / Guilty, we shall grow guilty by their deaths; / Their sins will light on us (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: Strike these men down, and only sin would cling to us — even though they have become aggressors
divergences.note: The crux of Arjuna's moral case. The Sanskrit atatayin is a precise legal-ethical term: an "aggressor" or assailant whom the law permits one to kill. Arjuna concedes the point — these men have wronged us — and then refuses anyway, holding that killing kin brings sin no matter how just the cause. Arnold's "if they be guilty" blurs this into a vaguer conditional. Keeping "aggressors" sharpens the dilemma: it is not that the war is unjust, but that even a just killing of one's own family is, for Arjuna, unbearable.

divergences.phrase: luptapindodaka-kriyah
divergences.older: Fall from their place of peace, being bereft / Of funeral-cakes and the wan death-water (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: robbed of the offerings of rice and water that are owed to the dead
divergences.note: Arjuna's argument turns on the shraddha rites: the dead depend on the living to offer pinda (balls of cooked rice) and udaka (water libations); without them the ancestors fall from their resting place. Arnold's "funeral-cakes" and "wan death-water" are evocative but obscure to a modern reader. We render the ritual plainly — "offerings of rice and water that are owed to the dead" — preserving the concrete content (this is why the destruction of a family is cosmic, not merely sentimental) without the Victorian archaism.

divergences.phrase: your right is to the work, not to its fruits (nishkama karma)
divergences.older: Arnold renders the teaching as "Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them," wrapped in a long passage about Brahmans drawing "text for all wants from tank of Holy Writ."
divergences.lectio: "So your concern is with the action itself, never with its fruits. Let the fruit of action never be your motive, and do not become attached to inaction either."
divergences.note: This is the Gita's most famous line and the seed of karma-yoga: act because the act is right, but renounce all claim on the result. The Sanskrit has a precise fourfold structure — you have a right to action, never to its fruits; let the fruit not be your motive; yet do not cling to inaction. Arnold dissolves the fourth clause into rhetoric; the Lectio edition restores its plain shape so the discipline (do the work, drop the reward, but do not down tools) stands clear.

divergences.phrase: as worn-out clothes are cast aside (the deathless atman changing bodies)
divergences.older: Arnold sets this as a lyric stanza: "Nay, but as when one layeth / His worn-out robes away, / And taking new ones, sayeth, / 'These will I wear to-day!' / So putteth by the spirit / Lightly its garb of flesh, / And passeth to inherit / A residence afresh."
divergences.lectio: "As a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on others that are new, so the self lays aside worn-out bodies and enters others that are new."
divergences.note: The chapter's central image of the imperishable Self (atman): the body dies, but the self that wears it does not. Arnold's archaic, sing-song quatrain ('layeth,' 'sayeth,' 'garb of flesh') makes the consolation feel quaint and distant. Rendered as plain prose, the simile keeps its full weight — death is a change of clothes, not an ending — without the Victorian costume.

divergences.phrase: the tortoise of withdrawn senses (sthitaprajna, the one of steady wisdom)
divergences.older: Arnold: "He who shall draw / As the wise tortoise draws its four feet safe / Under its shield, his five frail senses back / Under the spirit's buckler from the world / Which else assails them..."
divergences.lectio: "And when, like a tortoise drawing its limbs in under its shell, a person can draw his senses back from the things that tempt them, then his wisdom stands firm."
divergences.note: The Gita's portrait of the sage of steady wisdom (sthitaprajna), who can withdraw the senses at will. Arnold piles on apparatus — 'four feet,' 'shield,' 'five frail senses,' 'spirit's buckler' — that buries the simple, vivid image. The Lectio edition keeps the tortoise but lets it be a tortoise, so the comparison lands as cleanly in English as it does in the Sanskrit.

divergences.phrase: act as an offering, free of attachment
divergences.older: Arnold gives Krishna's charge as "such earthly duty do / Free from desire, and thou shalt well perform / Thy heavenly purpose," framing detached work as the road to a "heavenly purpose."
divergences.lectio: We render it as doing the work that is yours as an offering, free of attachment, because the one who works unattached reaches the highest.
divergences.note: The Sanskrit yajna is literal sacrifice. The chapter's hinge is that action done as offering (yajnartha karma) does not bind, while all other action does; Arnold's "heavenly purpose" abstracts this into vague piety. We keep the concrete language of offering so the load-bearing teaching — work without grasping at the fruit — stays visible.

divergences.phrase: for the holding-together of the world
divergences.older: Arnold renders lokasangraha variously as "the upholding of thy kind" and acting "to bring the world deliverance, and its bliss," tilting toward salvation.
divergences.lectio: We keep it as acting for the holding-together of the world, and acting so the wise hold the world together by their example, as Janaka did.
divergences.note: Lokasangraha is not "deliverance" but the keeping-together, the maintenance, of the social and cosmic order. The point is exemplary duty: what a great person does, others imitate (yad yad acarati shresthah). Arnold's "deliverance" imports a redemptive note the verse does not carry; the wise act to keep the world in order, not to save it.

divergences.phrase: better your own duty imperfectly than another's done well
divergences.older: Arnold: "this is better, that one do / His own task as he may, even though he fail, / Than take tasks not his own, though they seem good."
divergences.lectio: It is better to do your own duty imperfectly than to do another's duty well; better to die doing what is yours, for to take up another's work is dangerous.
divergences.note: This is svadharma, the chapter's most quoted line (shreyan svadharmo vigunah). The Sanskrit says another's duty is bhayavaha — frightening, perilous — not merely that one's own "fails." We restore the sharp edge: another's path, even done well, brings danger. Softening this loses the whole force of Krishna's answer to Arjuna's wish to lay down a warrior's work for an ascetic's.

divergences.phrase: desire and anger, the enemy that veils wisdom
divergences.older: Arnold names it "Kama... Passion... born of the Darknesses," and pictures wisdom "foiled, soiled, enclosed in this desire of flesh."
divergences.lectio: It is desire, it is anger, born of the force of passion — devouring, never satisfied, deeply corrupting; know this for the enemy. As smoke hides fire, as rust films a mirror, so wisdom is veiled by it.
divergences.note: The Sanskrit pairs kama (desire) and krodha (anger), born of rajas, the force of passion — Arnold's "Darknesses" wrongly suggests tamas (inertia). We name desire and anger plainly, keep both, and hold the three classic images (smoke, mirror, womb). Krishna's diagnosis — that desire, seated in senses, mind, and reason, is the one enemy that veils wisdom — is the climax of the chapter and must land without euphemism.

divergences.phrase: yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati bharata... dharma-samsthapanarthaya sambhavami yuge yuge
divergences.older: Arnold: "When Righteousness / Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness / Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take / Visible shape, and move a man with men, / Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back, / And setting Virtue on her seat again."
divergences.lectio: "For whenever dharma declines and the wrong prevails, Arjuna, I bring myself into being. Age after age I come into the world, in visible form, to protect the good, to destroy those who do evil, and to set dharma firmly in its place again."
divergences.note: The Gita's most famous teaching after 2.47: the doctrine of divine descent (avatara). The Sanskrit is precise and load-bearing and must not be softened — dharma (here kept as the term, not flattened to "Righteousness" or "Virtue"), its decline (glani), the rise of adharma, and the threefold purpose: protection of the good (paritranaya sadhunam), destruction of the wicked (vinashaya duskritam), and the re-establishment of dharma (dharma-samsthapana), "age after age" (yuge yuge). Arnold keeps the structure but dresses it in capitalized abstractions — "Righteousness," "Wickedness," "Virtue" on "her seat." We hold the concrete promise and keep dharma itself, because the whole weight of the verse rests on it: it is not a vague war of good and evil but the periodic restoration of the cosmic and moral order.

divergences.phrase: karmany akarma yah pashyed akarmani cha karma yah
divergences.older: Arnold: "He who sees / How action may be rest, rest action—he / Is wisest 'mid his kind; he hath the truth!"
divergences.lectio: "The one who can see inaction within action, and action within inaction, is the wise one among men; he is whole, and everything he does is done in the right spirit."
divergences.note: The chapter's signature paradox, and the key to its whole teaching on work. The point is not that action equals rest, as Arnold's "action may be rest, rest action" suggests, but that the sage who has renounced the fruit acts without being an agent — there is inaction (akarma) inside his action (karma) — while the one who merely sits still, his mind churning, is still acting. We keep the exact chiasmus of the Sanskrit (action in inaction, inaction in action) rather than collapsing it into "action and rest," because the precise crossing is the insight: freedom is not in stopping work but in the inner stillness within work.

divergences.phrase: yathaidhamsi samiddho 'gnir bhasmasat kurute 'rjuna jnanagnih sarva-karmani bhasmasat kurute tatha
divergences.older: Arnold: "As the kindled flame / Feeds on the fuel till it sinks to ash, / So unto ash, Arjuna! unto nought / The flame of Knowledge wastes works' dross away!"
divergences.lectio: "As a kindled fire turns its fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge turns all action to ashes."
divergences.note: The image that gives the chapter (Jnana-Yoga) its name: the fire of knowledge (jnana-agni) burns all karma to ash (bhasmasat). The Sanskrit says sarva-karmani — ALL actions, the whole accumulated weight of one's deeds — not merely the "dross" of works, as Arnold has it. The teaching is total: knowledge does not refine action, it consumes the binding power of action entirely. We keep "all action" and the plain, fierce image of fire reducing fuel to ash, so the climax of the chapter lands with its full force and sets up the closing command to cut doubt and rise.

divergences.phrase: as a lotus leaf is untouched by the water
divergences.older: He that acts in thought of Brahm, / Detaching end from act, with act content, / The world of sense can no more stain his soul / Than waters mar th' enamelled lotus-leaf. (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: Whoever acts laying all his actions on Brahman, having let go of attachment, is untouched by evil — as a lotus leaf is untouched by the water.
divergences.note: The single most famous image of the chapter: padma-patram ivambhasa, the lotus leaf untouched by the water it rests on. The Sanskrit verb is lipyate — to be smeared, stained, made to cling — and what does not cling to the karma-yogin is papena, evil or the residue of action. Arnold's "enamelled lotus-leaf" is pretty but adds a gloss the Sanskrit does not have, and his "world of sense" softens the point: it is not sensation that fails to stain the sage but the moral consequence of his deeds. We keep the plain miracle — water beading off a leaf and leaving it dry — because the whole teaching of acting-without-being-bound hangs on it.

divergences.phrase: the city with nine gates
divergences.older: The embodied sage, withdrawn within his soul, / At every act sits godlike in "the town / Which hath nine gateways," neither doing aught / Nor causing any deed. (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: Renouncing all actions with his mind, the one who has mastered himself sits at ease, the ruler of a city with nine gates, neither acting nor causing any action.
divergences.note: Nava-dvare pure dehi — the embodied self dwells in "a city of nine gates," the body with its nine openings (two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, mouth, and the two below). The point is that the self rules this city without being the doer within it: it neither acts nor sets action in motion (na eva kurvan na karayan). Arnold's "sits godlike" imports a grandeur the verse does not state; the force of the image is exactly the opposite — a quiet, restful sovereignty (aste sukham, "sits at ease"). We keep the literal city of nine gates, a load-bearing image, and the plain doubling that the sage is neither the one who acts nor the one who makes others act.

divergences.phrase: the same eye on a brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste
divergences.older: To him who wisely sees, / The Brahman with his scrolls and sanctities, / The cow, the elephant, the unclean dog, / The Outcast gorging dog's meat, are all one. (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: The learned, those who truly see, look with the same eye on a brahmin rich in learning and humility, on a cow, on an elephant, on a dog, and on an outcaste who lives by eating dogs.
divergences.note: The most radical line in the chapter: panditah sama-darshinah, the wise are "those who see the same." The Sanskrit lists, deliberately, the whole range of a caste-and-purity society — the learned brahmin (vidya-vinaya-sampanne, endowed with learning and humility), the cow, the elephant, the dog, and the shva-paka, the dog-cooker, the lowest outcaste — and says the wise look on all five with one undivided gaze. Arnold's "unclean dog" and "Outcast gorging dog's meat" load the lowest terms with disgust, which is precisely what the verse dissolves. We render the list straight, without contempt, so the equal vision (sama-darshana) lands as the scandal it is: the same self looks out of all of them.

divergences.phrase: uddhared atmanatmanam natmanam avasadayet — atmaiva hyatmano bandhur atmaiva ripur atmanah
divergences.older: Let each man raise / The Self by Soul, not trample down his Self, / Since Soul that is Self's friend may grow Self's foe (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: Let a man lift himself up by his own self, and never let himself sink down; for the self is the friend of the self, and the self is also its enemy.
divergences.note: The verse turns on a single word, atman, used over and over in different cases — the self that lifts and the self that is lifted, the self as friend and the self as foe. Arnold tries to split the pairing into two different words, "Self" and "Soul," which makes the reader hunt for a metaphysical distinction the Sanskrit does not draw: the whole point is that there is one self, and it can be its own rescuer or its own ruin depending on whether it is mastered. We keep the plain doubling — self lifting self — so the moral lands cleanly: no one elevates or debases you but you. This is the hinge of the chapter, the ground on which all the meditation that follows is built.

divergences.phrase: yatha deepo nivatastho nengate sopama smrita
divergences.older: Steadfast a lamp burns sheltered from the wind; / Such is the likeness of the Yogi's mind / Shut from sense-storms and burning bright to Heaven (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the image given for the disciplined yogi, his mind held in check, deep in the practice of communion with the self.
divergences.note: The most famous image of the chapter, and one that must be left exactly as the Sanskrit gives it: a flame in still air that does not waver. Arnold cannot resist gilding it — "burning bright to Heaven," "shut from sense-storms" — additions that bend a perfectly plain simile toward Victorian uplift. The text says only that the lamp does not flicker (na ingate), and that this is the very picture (upama) of the steadied mind. We give the image bare, because its power is in its quietness: the mind, like the flame, is simply still.

divergences.phrase: abhyasena tu kaunteya vairagyena ca grhyate — the restless mind, hard as the wind to hold, mastered by practice and dispassion
divergences.older: It were all one, I think, / To hold the wayward wind, as tame man's heart. ... Yet may it grow restrained by habit, Prince! / By wont of self-command (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: to hold it down seems to me as hard as holding down the wind. ... and yet, Arjuna, it can be held — by steady practice and by dispassion.
divergences.note: Arjuna's honest objection and Krishna's answer are the practical core of the chapter. Arnold keeps the wind image but renders Krishna's two remedies as "habit" and "wont of self-command," which flattens a precise pair of technical terms. The Sanskrit names them: abhyasa, sustained practice — doing the work again and again — and vairagya, dispassion, the loosening of one's grip on what the senses crave. Both are load-bearing and must stay distinct: practice trains the mind, dispassion empties it of the desires that make it restless in the first place. We keep "practice" and "dispassion" plainly, so the method survives the translation.

divergences.phrase: na hi kalyana-krt kascid durgatim tata gacchati — the seeker who falls short is reborn to take up the path again
divergences.older: He is not lost, thou Son of Pritha! No! ... and so he strives anew / To perfectness, with better hope, dear Prince! / For by the old desire he is drawn on / Unwittingly (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: no such man is lost, neither in this world nor in the world to come. For no one who does what is good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. ... There he recovers the understanding he had built up in his former body, and from that point he strives once more toward perfection.
divergences.note: Krishna's consolation to the seeker who dies before reaching the goal — the most tender passage in the chapter. The teaching is exact and must not be softened or lost: no sincere effort toward the good is ever wasted (na hi kalyana-krt kascid durgatim... gacchati), and the practice already done carries over into the next birth, where the seeker resumes from where he left off. Arnold's version is faithful in substance but wrapped in endearments ("dear Prince," "with better hope") and inversions that blur the plain promise. We keep the promise itself sharp and unhedged, because it is the chapter's answer to despair: the path is never broken off, only continued.

divergences.phrase: para and apara prakriti — the higher and lower natures
divergences.older: Arnold: "Earth, water, flame, air, ether, life, and mind, / And individuality—those eight / Make up the showing of Me, Manifest. / These be my lower Nature; learn the higher, / Whereby... this Universe / Is, by its principle of life, produced."
divergences.lectio: "...this is my nature, divided eightfold. But this is only my lower nature, Arjuna. Know that I have another, a higher nature: the very principle of life, by which this whole world is held up and sustained."
divergences.note: The structural backbone of the chapter: Krishna divides his prakriti (nature) in two. The lower (apara) is the eightfold material world — earth, water, fire, air, ether, plus mind, intellect, and ahankara (the sense of "I"). The higher (para) is the jiva-bhuta, the life-principle that animates and upholds the world (yayedam dharyate jagat). Arnold renders the eight as "the showing of Me, Manifest" and keeps "lower" and "higher" Nature, but blurs the precise contrast of para/apara into atmosphere. We keep the two natures plainly opposed and load-bearing, because the whole theology of the chapter — that God is both the inert stuff of the world and the life within it — rests on this division.

divergences.phrase: raso 'ham apsu kaunteya — I am the taste in water
divergences.older: Arnold: "I am the fresh taste of the water; I / The silver of the moon, the gold o' the sun, / The word of worship in the Veds, the thrill / That passeth in the ether, and the strength / Of man's shed seed."
divergences.lectio: "I am the taste in water, Arjuna; I am the light in the moon and the sun; I am the sacred syllable OM that sounds in all the Vedas, the sound in the air, the manhood in men. I am the pure scent of the earth and the brightness in fire; I am the life in all that lives..."
divergences.note: The great litany of the chapter, where Krishna names himself the essence within each thing — rasa, the taste in water; prabha, the light in sun and moon; pranava, the syllable OM in the Vedas; shabda, the sound in air; paurusha, the manhood in men; the scent of earth, the brightness of fire, the life in all beings. Arnold keeps the incantation but gilds and scatters it: "the silver of the moon, the gold o' the sun," "the thrill that passeth in the ether," the coy "strength / Of man's shed seed." We keep the bare anaphora — "I am... I am... I am" — and the proper noun OM, because the force of the passage is incantatory: a single divine presence named, item by item, as the inwardness of the whole sensible world.

divergences.phrase: daivi hy esha guna-mayi mama maya duratyaya — this divine illusion of mine is hard to cross
divergences.older: Arnold: "Hard it is / To pierce that veil divine of various shows / Which hideth Me; yet they who worship Me / Pierce it and pass beyond."
divergences.lectio: "For this divine illusion of mine, this maya woven of the three qualities, is hard to see past; only those who take refuge in me alone pass beyond it."
divergences.note: The Gita's first sustained use of maya as the veiling power of God. The Sanskrit is precise: the illusion is daivi (divine, belonging to God), guna-mayi (made of the three gunas), and duratyaya (very hard to cross over). It is pierced not by effort or cleverness but only by taking refuge in Krishna himself (mam eva ye prapadyante). Arnold keeps "veil divine" and "pierce it," but drops the key term itself. We keep maya as the term — it is load-bearing, the name of the whole problem the chapter sets — and keep the one remedy plain: not insight but surrender.

divergences.phrase: the four who worship, and the jnani dearest
divergences.older: Arnold: "Four sorts of mortals know me: he who weeps... and the man who yearns to know; / And he who toils to help; and he who sits / Certain of me, enlightened... highest, nearest, best / That last is, the devout soul, wise, intent / Upon 'The One.' Dear, above all, am I / To him; and he is dearest unto me!"
divergences.lectio: "Four kinds of good people turn to me in worship, Arjuna: the one in distress, the one who seeks knowledge, the one who seeks some good of his own, and the one who already knows. Of these, the one who knows — the wise one, ever steadfast, devoted to the one alone — stands highest; for I am dear above all things to the wise, and he is dear to me."
divergences.note: The famous fourfold catalogue of devotees: the arta (the distressed), the jijnasu (the seeker of knowledge), the artharthin (the seeker of some good or wealth), and the jnani (the one who knows). All four are called good (sukritinah), but the jnani is dearest, because he loves God for nothing beyond God — ekabhakti, devoted to the one alone. Arnold catches the substance ("he who weeps," "he who yearns to know," "he who toils to help," the "enlightened") but his loose paraphrase obscures the deliberate ranking. We keep the four distinct and the jnani plainly first, with the mutual dearness intact (priyo hi jnanino 'tyartham aham sa cha mama priyah) — the tenderest line in the chapter, where God and the one who knows him are dear to each other.

divergences.phrase: yam yam vapi smaran bhavam tyajaty ante kalevaram tam tam evaiti
divergences.older: Arnold: "But, if he meditated otherwise / At hour of death, in putting off the flesh, / He goes to what he looked for, Kunti's Son! / Because the Soul is fashioned to its like."
divergences.lectio: But whatever state a person dwells on as he leaves the body at the end, to that state he goes, Arjuna, having been shaped by it all his life long.
divergences.note: The load-bearing teaching of the chapter, and the reason for the whole discipline that follows. The Sanskrit is exact: whatever state of being (bhava) one is dwelling on (smaran) at the moment of leaving the body, to that very state (tam tam eva) one goes. The crucial closing phrase, sada tad-bhava-bhavitah, says this is no last-second accident — one arrives there having been formed by that state always, across a whole life. Arnold's "the Soul is fashioned to its like" gestures at this but blurs it; we keep the plain mechanism — you become what you have made your mind dwell on — because it is the hinge on which "remember me and fight" turns.

divergences.phrase: om ity ekaksharam brahma — uttering OM, the sacred syllable, at the hour of death
divergences.older: Arnold: "And, murmuring OM, the sacred syllable— / Emblem of BRAHM—dies, meditating Me."
divergences.lectio: and who, uttering the single sacred syllable OM — the sound of Brahman — keeps me in mind as he goes out from the body: that person walks the highest road.
divergences.note: The chapter's concrete discipline of dying: the gates of the senses shut, the mind penned in the heart, the life-breath (prana) drawn up into the head, the single syllable OM on the lips. OM itself (om ity ekaksharam brahma — "OM, the one syllable, is Brahman") is preserved untranslated; it is not a symbol of Brahman but, in the text, Brahman in sound. Arnold's "Emblem of BRAHM" softens this into mere emblem and inverts the death into a passive "dies." We keep OM as the sacred syllable it is and keep the act deliberate — the dying yogi utters it — because the practice is load-bearing and physical, not figurative.

divergences.phrase: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar... the day and night of Brahma, and the unmanifest beyond the unmanifest
divergences.older: Arnold: "If ye know Brahma's Day / Which is a thousand Yugas... But—higher, deeper, innermost—abides / Another Life... This is that Life named the Unmanifest, / The Infinite! the All! the Uttermost. / Thither arriving none return."
divergences.lectio: When that long day dawns, all things come forth into the visible world out of the unmanifest... But beyond this unmanifest there is another, a higher unmanifest still, everlasting, which does not perish when all things perish.
divergences.note: The cosmology of time, and the chapter's deepest distinction. A day of Brahma is a thousand ages (yugas), and his night as long; at dawn all beings stream out of the unmanifest (avyakta), at nightfall they dissolve back into it — helplessly (avashah), the same beings over and over. But the Sanskrit then names a second unmanifest, avyaktat tu parah — "higher than the unmanifest" — eternal and imperishable, which does not die when all beings die (yah sa sarveshu bhuteshu nashyatsu na vinashyati). Arnold keeps the doctrine but his piled-up exclamations ("The Infinite! the All! the Uttermost") flatten the precise two-tier structure. We hold the distinction clear: there is the unmanifest from which worlds rise and fall, and beyond it the imperishable ground that abides through all dissolution — the supreme goal from which there is no return.

divergences.phrase: shukla-krishne gati hy ete jagatah shashvate mate — the bright path and the dark path
divergences.older: Arnold's text omits these verses entirely (the gap marked "..." in his Chapter VIII), passing from the cosmology straight to the closing praise of wisdom.
divergences.lectio: Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight of the waxing moon, the six months of the sun's northern journey — those who know Brahman and go out by this path go on to Brahman. Smoke, the night, the dark fortnight of the waning moon, the six months of the sun's southern journey — by this path the disciplined one reaches only the light of the moon, and returns.
divergences.note: The chapter's signature image, and one Arnold simply drops. The Sanskrit gives two everlasting ways (gati) by which a soul leaves the world: the bright path — fire, flame, daylight, the waxing moon, the sun's northern course (uttarayana) — by which the knowers of Brahman go and do not return (anavritti); and the dark path — smoke, night, the waning moon, the southern course (dakshinayana) — by which the soul reaches the moon's light and comes back again (avartate punah). We restore the whole sequence in full, because the two paths are the load-bearing teaching the chapter has been building toward — light leading to no-return, smoke leading to return — and to leave them out, as Arnold does, is to lose the point of the cosmology that precedes them.

divergences.phrase: matsthani sarvabhutani na caham tesv avasthitah... na ca matsthani bhutani
divergences.older: In Me are all existences contained; / Not I in them! ... Yet they are not contained, / Those visible things!... My Being— / Creating all, sustaining all—still dwells / Outside of all! (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: All beings rest in me, but I am not in them. And yet they do not rest in me either — look on this, the mystery of my power: my self gives birth to all beings and sustains them, and still it does not dwell within them.
divergences.note: The signature paradox of the chapter, and the hardest line in the Gita: all beings rest in Krishna (matsthani sarvabhutani), yet he is not in them (na caham tesu), and in the next breath they do not even rest in him (na ca matsthani bhutani). The Sanskrit holds the contradiction open on purpose — the commentators (Shankara, Ramanuja) read it as a 'relationless relation,' the way space contains all things without being touched by them. Arnold keeps both halves but pads them with 'visible things,' 'My Being,' and 'dwells outside of all,' which resolves the tension toward a tidy transcendence. We keep all three clauses bare and in their stark order — in me / not in me / not even in me — because the teaching lives in the refusal to collapse the paradox: the divine is the ground of everything and yet bound to nothing, immanent and untouched at once.

divergences.phrase: yathakasa-sthito nityam vayuh sarvatra-go mahan
divergences.older: See! as the shoreless airs / Move in the measureless space, but are not space, / [And space were space without the moving airs]; / So all things are in Me, but are not I. (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: As the mighty wind moves everywhere, yet always remains within space, so all beings remain within me. Understand this.
divergences.note: The image that makes the paradox bearable: the great wind (mahan vayuh) ranges over the whole world yet never leaves the space (akasha) that holds it. The point is containment without confinement — the wind is in space, space is not in the wind. Arnold cannot leave it alone: he adds a whole bracketed line of his own invention ('And space were space without the moving airs') and turns the verse into a small philosophical argument about whether space needs the wind. The Sanskrit simply gives the picture and says: so all beings rest in me. We strip Arnold's interpolation entirely and keep the plain simile, because its force is in its quietness — the wind goes everywhere and is still always within the sky.

divergences.phrase: patram puspam phalam toyam yo me bhaktya prayacchati
divergences.older: Whoso shall offer Me in faith and love / A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water poured forth, / That offering I accept, lovingly made / With pious will. (Arnold, 1885)
divergences.lectio: Whoever offers me, with love, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of love, made by the pure of heart, I gladly accept.
divergences.note: The most beloved verse of the chapter, and the heart of its democracy of devotion: not soma, not the costly fire-rite of the three Vedas, but a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water (patram, puspam, phalam, toyam) — whatever the poorest hand can hold — is enough, if it is offered with love (bhaktya). Arnold's rendering is close and we keep his four objects exactly, but his 'water poured forth' and 'pious will' lean Victorian. We hold the four plain things in their bare list and let the load-bearing word stand twice: it is the love, not the gift, that Krishna receives. This single verse answers the whole machinery of sacrifice the chapter has just described, and sets up the promise four verses on that even the lowliest, turning to him in love, reach the highest.

segments.text: Dhritarashtra said: On the sacred plain of Kurukshetra, drawn up and hungry for battle — tell me, Sanjaya: what did my people do, and what did the sons of Pandu do?

Sanjaya said: When he saw the army of the Pandavas arrayed for war, King Duryodhana went to his teacher Drona and said: "Master, look at this great host of Pandu's sons, marshalled by the son of Drupada, your own pupil in the art of war. Here stand heroes, great archers, the equals of Bhima and Arjuna in battle — Yuyudhana, Virata, and Drupada the mighty charioteer; Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, and the valiant king of Kashi; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saivya, that bull among men; bold Yudhamanyu and brave Uttamaujas; the son of Subhadra, and the sons of Draupadi — every one of them a great warrior, mounted on his shining chariot.

"Know, too, best of Brahmins, the finest of our own side — the captains of my army. Let me name them, so you may recognize them: yourself first of all, then Bhishma and Karna, and Kripa ever victorious in the fight; Ashvatthaman, Vikarna, and the son of Somadatta as well — and many another hero besides, each armed with his chosen weapon, all skilled in war, every one of them ready this day to lay down his life for me. Yet our forces, guarded by Bhishma, seem to me too few, while theirs, guarded by Bhima, seem strong enough. So let all of you, standing each in his place along the line, give support to Bhishma above all."

Then, to lift the old king's heart, the eldest of the Kurus, Bhishma, raised his conch and sounded a blast like a lion's roar. At once conches and kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and trumpets broke out all together, and the sound was a tumult. Then, standing in their great chariot yoked with white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blew their divine conches. Krishna sounded the conch called Panchajanya, and Arjuna the one called Devadatta; Bhima of the terrible deeds, the wolf-bellied, blew his great conch Paundra. King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, sounded Anantavijaya, "Endless Victory"; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosha, the "Sweet-toned," and Manipushpaka, the "Jewel-flowered." The great archer who is king of Kashi, and Shikhandi the mighty charioteer, Dhrishtadyumna and Virata and Satyaki the unconquered, Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, and the strong-armed son of Subhadra — all of them, lord of the earth, blew their conches, each his own. And that din tore through the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons, until heaven and earth themselves seemed to shake with the roar.

Then, seeing Dhritarashtra's men drawn up and the clash of weapons about to begin, Arjuna — whose banner bore the figure of Hanuman the monkey — lifted his bow and said to Krishna: "Unshaken One, drive my chariot out into the open ground between the two armies, that I may look closely at these men gathered here, eager for battle, and see with whom I must contend in this coming fight. Let me see them, those who have come together here ready to do the bidding in war of the wicked-minded son of Dhritarashtra."

So spoken to by Arjuna, Krishna drove that splendid chariot out into the space between the armies, and halted it before Bhishma and Drona and all the kings of the earth. "Behold, Arjuna," he said, "the Kurus gathered here." And there Arjuna saw them standing — fathers and grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and grandsons, comrades, fathers-in-law, and dear friends, in both armies alike. Seeing all these kinsmen arrayed against him, Arjuna was overcome with deep pity, and in his sorrow he said:

Arjuna said: Krishna, when I look on these, my own people, gathered here and longing to fight, my limbs give way and my mouth goes dry; my body shakes and my hair stands on end. Gandiva, my great bow, slips from my hand, and my very skin is on fire. I cannot stand; my mind is reeling. And I see nothing but evil omens, Krishna. No good can come of killing my own kin in battle. I have no wish for victory, Krishna, nor for kingship, nor for pleasures. What is a kingdom to us, Govinda, what are delights, or life itself, when the very men for whose sake we would want kingdom and delight and pleasure are standing here in the line of battle, ready to give up their lives and their wealth — teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers too; uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and all our kin? Even if they kill me, Krishna, I would not want to kill them — not for the lordship of all three worlds, much less for this earth.

What joy could be ours, Krishna, in killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Strike these men down, and only sin would cling to us — even though they have become aggressors. So we have no right to slay our own kinsmen, the sons of Dhritarashtra; for how could we ever be happy, Krishna, having killed our own people? Even if they, with minds blinded by greed, see no wrong in the ruin of a family or the betrayal of friends, why should we not have the wisdom to turn back from this crime — we who can see plainly the evil that comes of destroying a family? For when a family is destroyed, its ancient ways perish with it; and when the old ways are gone, lawlessness overtakes the whole house. With lawlessness, Krishna, the women of the family are corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, the order of castes breaks down. And that confusion drags the destroyers of the family, and the family itself, down into hell; for their ancestors fall from their place, robbed of the offerings of rice and water that are owed to the dead. By these crimes of the family-destroyers, which throw the castes into confusion, the eternal ways of caste and of the household are wiped out. And we have heard, Krishna, that for those whose household ways are wiped out, a dwelling in hell is certain. Alas, that we should be ready to commit so great a sin — that, out of greed for the joys of kingship, we are prepared to kill our own people! Better by far that the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, should kill me in the battle, unresisting and unarmed.
Having spoken thus on the field of battle, Arjuna sank down upon the seat of his chariot, letting his bow and arrows fall, his heart overwhelmed with grief.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: The Deathless Self and the Way of Action

segments.text: Sanjaya: To Arjuna, overcome with such pity and such grief, his eyes blurred with tears, his spirit broken, the charioteer Madhusudana spoke these stern words.

Krishna: Where has this weakness come from, here at the worst hour? It is unworthy of you, it shames a brave man, it shuts you out of the noble path. Have done with this faintness, Arjuna. It does not become you. Shake off this cowardly mood, stand up, and be yourself again, scourge of your enemies.
Arjuna: But how, Krishna, am I to aim my arrows in battle against Bhishma and Drona? They are men worthy of my reverence, men I am bound to honor.

It would be better to live in this world on a beggar's crust than to kill these great souls, my teachers; for if I struck them down, every pleasure I tasted afterward would be smeared with their blood. And which is the worse outcome — that we should win, or that they should — I cannot even say. The very men whose death would leave my life empty are standing there before me, drawn up for war. My whole nature is unstrung with pity, my mind clouded over about what is right; so I ask you plainly, tell me which course is better. I am your pupil; I throw myself on your guidance — teach me. For I can see nothing that would drive out the grief that is scorching my senses, not if I won an unrivaled and prosperous kingdom over the whole earth, nor even lordship over the gods.

Sanjaya: So Arjuna spoke to Krishna, the lord of hearts; and then, saying, "I will not fight," he fell silent. To him, standing crushed between the two armies, Krishna answered, with the trace of a smile.

Krishna: You grieve where no grief is called for, and the words you speak, for all their sound of wisdom, are unwise. The truly wise mourn neither for the living nor for the dead. There was never a time when I was not, nor you, nor any of these princes; and there will never be a time hereafter when any of us shall cease to be. As the self within this body passes through childhood and youth and old age, so too at death it passes on into another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this. It is only the contact of the senses with their objects, Arjuna, that brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain; these come and go, they do not last — so endure them. The man whom these cannot shake, who takes pain and pleasure alike with an even mind, is fit for what does not die.

What is real can never cease to be; what is unreal never truly is. The men who have seen to the bottom of things have seen the truth of both — they have learned to tell the abiding substance from the passing shadow. Know that the power which spreads itself through everything cannot be destroyed; no one can bring an end to this, the imperishable. It is only the bodies that wear out — the bodies that house this eternal, indestructible, measureless self. Therefore fight, Arjuna. The man who imagines that the self can be a killer, and the man who supposes that the self can be killed — neither of them understands. It does not kill, and it cannot be killed.

It is never born, and it never dies; having once been, it never ceases to be. Unborn, undying, ancient and unchanging, it is not slain when the body is slain. How can a man who knows it to be indestructible, unborn, deathless, beyond all change — how can such a man kill anyone, or cause any killing?

As a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on others that are new, so the self lays aside worn-out bodies and enters others that are new. Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot drench it, the wind cannot dry it. It cannot be pierced or burned or soaked or withered; it is unchanging, present everywhere, steady and sure. It is unseen, beyond all thought, beyond all change. Knowing it to be such, you have no reason to grieve.

And even if you were to hold that the self is endlessly born and endlessly dies, you would still have no cause to mourn, Arjuna; for then, to whatever is born, death is certain, and to whatever dies, birth is certain — so why grieve over what cannot be helped? Creatures are unseen before their birth and unseen again after their death, and seen only in between. What is there in this to mourn over? One person looks on the self as a marvel, another speaks of it as a marvel, another hears of it as a marvel — and even having heard, not one of them truly knows it. This self, dwelling in the body of every living thing, can never be harmed; so you have no reason, Arjuna, to grieve for any creature.

Look, too, at your own duty, and do not waver; for a warrior there is no higher good than a war waged for what is right. Lucky are the warriors, Arjuna, to whom such a battle comes unsought, an open door into heaven. But if you refuse this just and honorable fight, then you throw away your own duty and your good name, and you take on guilt. People will tell of your disgrace forever after, and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death. The great captains will think you fled the field out of fear, and those who held you in high regard will hold you cheap. Your enemies will mock your courage with bitter words — and what could be more painful than that? If you are killed, you will gain heaven; if you win, you will enjoy the earth. So stand up, son of Kunti, resolved to fight.

Treat pleasure and pain as one, gain and loss as one, victory and defeat as one; then gird yourself for battle, and so doing you will take on no guilt. What I have told you so far is the wisdom of analysis, of Sankhya. Now hear the wisdom of Yoga, of action — once you hold to it, you will throw off the bondage of your deeds. On this path no effort is ever wasted and no step is ever lost; even a little of this practice rescues a person from the greatest fear. Here there is one resolve, single and steady; but the minds of the irresolute branch out endlessly in every direction.

There are foolish people who delight in the mere letter of the scriptures, who say there is nothing more to be had than this. Their hearts are full of craving; they make heaven their goal; their ornate rituals promise rich rebirths as the reward of their good deeds, and aim only at pleasure and power. But those who cling so to pleasure and power never settle their minds in steady contemplation. The scriptures deal with the three qualities of nature; rise above those three qualities, Arjuna — free yourself from the play of opposites, abide always in pure being, take no anxious thought for getting and keeping, and rest at peace in the self. To one who truly knows, the scriptures are worth no more than a well in a country flooded with water. So your concern is with the action itself, never with its fruits. Let the fruit of action never be your motive, and do not become attached to inaction either.

Stand firm in this discipline, Arjuna, and do your work, letting go of all attachment, holding success and failure to be one and the same; for this even-mindedness is what is meant by Yoga. Action done for its fruit is far inferior to action done in this even-minded discipline; seek refuge in that steadiness of mind. Pitiful are those who labor only for a reward. The person whose mind is disciplined in this way casts off both good and evil deeds even in this life; so give yourself to this discipline, for skill in action is exactly this discipline. The wise, disciplined in mind, renounce the fruit that their deeds would earn them, and so they are set free from the bondage of birth and pass to the place beyond all suffering. When your understanding has crossed clear of the thicket of confusion, you will grow indifferent to all the doctrine you have heard or have yet to hear. When your mind, once bewildered by competing teachings, stands unshaken and steady in deep contemplation, then you will have reached this discipline.
Arjuna: And how, Krishna, do we know the person whose wisdom is steady, whose mind rests firm in contemplation? How does such a person speak, how sit, how move?

Krishna: When a person lets go of every desire that haunts the mind, son of Pritha, and finds in the self alone all the contentment he needs, then his wisdom is steady. The one whose mind is not shaken in sorrow, who does not hunger after pleasure, who is free of longing and fear and anger — he is the sage of steady wisdom. The one who clings to nothing anywhere, who neither rejoices in good fortune nor recoils from bad, has settled his wisdom firmly. And when, like a tortoise drawing its limbs in under its shell, a person can draw his senses back from the things that tempt them, then his wisdom stands firm.

The objects of sense may fall away from a person who refuses to feed on them, yet the taste for them can linger; but even that last taste falls away once he has glimpsed the highest. For the senses are turbulent, Arjuna; they can carry off by force even the mind of one who strives and knows. Let him hold them all in check and sit intent on me; for the person who has mastered his senses is the one whose wisdom stands firm. When a person dwells on the objects of sense, attachment to them springs up; from attachment grows desire, and from desire flares anger. From anger comes confusion; from confusion the memory fails; when memory fails, the understanding is lost; and when the understanding is lost, the person is ruined.

But the disciplined soul, moving among the objects of sense with senses freed from craving and aversion, mastered and under his own control, comes to serenity; and in that serenity all his sorrows are dissolved, for the mind of one at peace soon grows steady in wisdom. The undisciplined have no such wisdom, and no power of steady thought; without steady thought there is no peace, and without peace, where is happiness to be found? When the mind runs after the roving senses and lets one of them carry it off, that one bears away a person's wisdom as a gale drives a ship off course across the water. Therefore, Arjuna, the one whose senses are reined in on every side from their objects — his wisdom stands firm.

What is night to all other creatures is the waking hour of the self-mastered; and what is the waking world to other creatures is night to the seer who truly sees. As the waters pour into the ocean, which stays full and unmoved even while they enter it, so all desires may flow into the one who is at peace — and that person, not the man who chases after his desires, attains peace. The one who has given up every desire and moves through the world without longing, without grasping, without any thought of "I" and "mine," comes to peace. This is the state of Brahman, Arjuna; once a person reaches it he is no longer deluded, and to stand firm in it even at the hour of death is to pass into the peace of God.

Arjuna said: If you hold that the way of understanding is higher than the way of action, Janardana, then why, Kesava, do you urge me into this terrible deed? Your words seem to point two ways at once, and they leave me confused. Tell me plainly, settle it for me: which single road leads to what is best?

Krishna said: I told you, blameless one, that in this world there are two paths, two disciplines of wisdom. There is the way of knowledge, which the followers of Sankhya walk through clear reflection; and there is the way of action, the discipline of work. But these are not finally two. No one escapes action by refusing to act, and no one reaches perfection by renunciation alone.

In fact no one can stay still even for a moment without acting. Everyone is driven to act, helpless under the forces of their own nature. The man who sits rigidly holding his body still while his mind keeps circling the very things he has given up is fooling no one but himself; he is a hypocrite. But the man who keeps his senses in hand and turns his powers to honest work, without grasping at any reward — that man, Arjuna, is the one to honor. So do the work that is yours to do. Action is better than inaction; without it you could not even keep your body alive.

There is, however, a kind of work that binds the soul, and a kind that sets it free. Only work done as an offering escapes the chain; all other work shackles the world to it. So, Arjuna, do your work as an offering, free of attachment. At the beginning, when the Lord of creatures made humankind, he made sacrifice along with them, and said: By this you shall flourish; let this be the cow that grants every wish. By it nourish the gods, and let the gods nourish you; sustaining one another, you will reach the highest good. Fed by your offerings, the gods will give you the food you need; but whoever takes their gifts and gives nothing back is no better than a thief.

The good eat what is left after the offering is made, and they are freed of fault; but those who cook only for themselves feed on their own wrongdoing. All living things are sustained by food, food comes from the rain, rain comes from sacrifice, and sacrifice arises from action. Know that action springs from the sacred order itself, and that the sacred, all-pervading, is forever present in every offering. Whoever does not help to turn this wheel as it was set turning, but lives only to gratify his senses, lives a wasted and shameful life.

But the one who finds his joy in the Self, who is content and satisfied within the Self, has nothing left that he needs to do. He has no stake in what is done or left undone here, and depends on no other creature for anything. So do the work that falls to you, but always without attachment; for the one who works unattached reaches the highest. It was through action alone that Janaka and others of old attained perfection. And you should act, if only for the holding-together of the world. Whatever a great man does, ordinary people imitate; the standard he sets, the whole world follows.

Look at me, son of Pritha. In all three worlds there is nothing I am bound to do, nothing left for me to gain or reach — and yet I keep acting. For if I did not go on working, tireless and watchful, people everywhere would follow my example; the human race would take me as its excuse and fall into ruin, and I would be the cause of confusion and the undoing of these creatures. So, just as the ignorant act because they are bound to their work, the wise should act too — but unattached, working to hold the world together. Let the wise not unsettle the minds of the ignorant who are still bound to their work; rather, doing all things with discipline, let the wise make such work attractive.

Everything that happens is the work of nature's own forces; only a man fooled by his pride imagines, "I am the one who acts." But the one who sees the truth of how these forces and their work move among the senses keeps himself apart, knowing it is the forces acting upon the forces, not the Self. Those deceived by nature's forces cling to their work; let the one who knows the whole not unsettle these others who know only a part. So surrender all your actions to me, fix your mind on the Self, and fight — with no craving, no sense of "mine," and the fever gone out of you.

Those who keep faith with this teaching of mine and act on it without complaint are freed from the bondage of their actions. But those who carp at my teaching and refuse to act on it — know them for fools, blind to all real understanding, and lost. Even the wise act according to their own nature; every creature follows its nature, and what good does it do to fight it? The senses are bound to be drawn toward what they like and pushed from what they dislike; do not fall under the power of these two, for they are the ambush set across your path.
It is better to do your own duty imperfectly than to do another's duty well. Better to die doing what is yours to do; to take up another's work is dangerous.
Arjuna said: But then what is it, Krishna, that drives a man to do wrong even against his own will, as though some force were pushing him into it?

Krishna said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the force of passion in us — devouring, never satisfied, deeply corrupting. Know this for the enemy. As smoke hides fire, as rust films over a mirror, as the womb wraps the unborn child, so is wisdom veiled by this. Knowledge itself is veiled, Arjuna, by this steady enemy of the wise — desire, that burns on like a fire and is never filled. The senses, the mind, and the reason are said to be its seat; through these it veils wisdom and deludes the embodied soul. So first take hold of your senses, son of Bharata, and strike this thing down, this destroyer of wisdom and understanding. The senses are strong, they say; stronger than the senses is the mind; stronger than the mind is the reason; but stronger than the reason is the Self. So know the Self, which is higher than reason; steady yourself by your own deeper self, and kill this enemy, Arjuna — desire, so hard to corner and overcome.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: The Way of Knowledge and Sacrifice

segments.text: Krishna said: This undying discipline, this deep union, I once taught to Vivasvat, the lord of light; Vivasvat handed it down to Manu, and Manu to Ikshvaku, and so it passed from king to king along a line of royal sages. But over the long stretch of years the teaching was worn away and finally lost. Now I declare that same ancient discipline to you, this supreme secret, because you are devoted to me and you are my friend.
Arjuna said: But you were born in our own day, and Vivasvat lived ages ago. How am I to understand that it was you who taught it at the very beginning?

Krishna said: You and I have both passed through many births, Arjuna. I remember them all; you do not. Though I am unborn, deathless, and beyond all change, though I am the lord of every living thing, still I take on birth by my own power, holding sway over the nature that is mine. For whenever dharma declines and the wrong prevails, Arjuna, I bring myself into being. Age after age I come into the world, in visible form, to protect the good, to destroy those who do evil, and to set dharma firmly in its place again. The one who truly knows this — the truth of my births and of my work — is not born again when he leaves the body behind; he comes to me. Many have already come to me this way: rid of longing, fear, and anger, made wholly mine, taking refuge in me, made pure by the fire of knowledge. However people approach me, I welcome them on that same path; for whatever road they take, Arjuna, it is my road in the end. Those who long for their works to bear fruit make their offerings to the gods, because in this human world the fruits of action come quickly. It was I who brought forth the four orders of society, dividing them according to their qualities and their work; yet though I am its maker, know me also as the one who does nothing and never changes. Actions do not stain me, for I have no craving for their fruit. Whoever understands me in this way is not bound by his own actions either. Knowing this, the seekers of old did their work and won their freedom. So you too should work, as your forebears worked long ago.

Even the wise are puzzled about what action is and what inaction is. So I will explain to you what action is, and once you know it you will be set free from all that is wrong. You must understand three things — what action is, what wrong action is, and what inaction is — for the workings of action run deep and dark. The one who can see inaction within action, and action within inaction, is the wise one among men; he is whole, and everything he does is done in the right spirit. The one whose every undertaking is free of the grasping of desire, whose works are burned clean in the fire of knowledge — the wise call that man wise. He gives up all claim on the fruit of his deeds; he is always content, leaning on nothing; and though he is fully at work, in truth he does nothing at all. Wanting nothing, his mind and his deeper self held in check, letting go of everything he might possess, he takes on no fault though his body acts. Content with whatever comes to him, beyond the pull of opposites, free of envy, the same whether he succeeds or fails — he is not bound, even as he acts. For one who is free, whose mind rests in knowledge, who does all his work as an offering, every trace of his action dissolves away.

When such a person makes an offering, the act of offering is Brahman, and what is offered is Brahman; Brahman pours it into the fire that is Brahman; and Brahman is what he reaches, since in all his work he keeps his mind fixed on Brahman. Some who follow this discipline offer sacrifice to the gods; others offer the self itself into the fire of Brahman. Some pour their hearing and their other senses into the fires of restraint; others pour sound and the rest of what the senses crave into the fires of the senses. Still others offer up all the workings of their senses and their breath into the fire of self-mastery, kindled by knowledge. Some make their offering with their wealth, some with hard discipline, some with the practice of yoga; and others, men of strict vows, offer their study of the sacred word and the knowledge it brings. There are those, intent on the breath, who offer the outgoing breath into the incoming, and the incoming into the outgoing, holding the flow of both in check; and those who fast, cutting back on food, and so pour breath into breath. All of these understand what sacrifice is, and by their offerings their faults are washed away. Those who eat the sacred remnant that is left after the offering pass on to the eternal Brahman; but for the one who offers nothing, even this world is closed — how then could the next be his, best of men?

Offerings of every kind lie open before Brahman. Know that they are all born of action; once you understand this, you will be free. But the offering made of knowledge is worth more than any offering of mere things, Arjuna; for all action, without exception, finds its fulfillment in knowledge. Learn it by bowing low, by asking honestly, by giving service; the wise, who have seen the truth, will hand that knowledge on to you. Once you know it, you will never fall back into such confusion again; for by this knowledge you will see every living thing within yourself, and so within me. Even if you were the worst sinner of all sinners, the boat of knowledge would carry you safely across every wrong you have done. As a kindled fire turns its fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge turns all action to ashes. There is nothing in this world so cleansing as knowledge; the one who has grown ripe in this discipline finds it, in time, within his own self. The man of faith, who is intent on it and holds his senses in check, gains this knowledge; and once he has it, he comes swiftly to the highest peace. But the man who is ignorant, who has no faith, whose nature is all doubt, is lost. For the doubting soul there is neither this world nor the next, nor any happiness anywhere. Actions cannot bind the one who has given up his deeds through the discipline of yoga, whose doubt has been cut away by knowledge, who has come home to himself, Arjuna. So with the sword of knowledge cut down this doubt that springs from ignorance and lodges in your heart. Take up the discipline, Arjuna, and stand up and fight.
Arjuna said: One moment, Krishna, you praise the giving up of action; the next, you praise action done in discipline. Tell me plainly, settle it for me: which of these two is the better way?

Krishna said: To give up action and to do action in discipline both lead to the highest good; but of the two, the discipline of action is better than the giving up of action. Know that the true renouncer is the one who neither hungers for anything nor recoils from anything; free of the play of opposites, he is set loose from bondage easily, Arjuna. It is only the unschooled who speak of the way of knowledge and the way of action as two separate things; the wise know better. Whoever is established in one of them gains the fruit of both. The state that the followers of knowledge reach is reached by the followers of action as well; whoever sees that the two ways are one sees truly.

But renunciation by itself, Arjuna, is hard to come by without the discipline of action; the sage made one with that discipline reaches Brahman before long. The one who is so disciplined, whose self is pure, who has mastered his body and his senses, whose self has become the self of all that lives — such a person is not stained even while he acts. "I do nothing at all," the disciplined one thinks, who knows the truth of things — for in seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, letting go, taking hold, opening and closing his eyes, he holds throughout that it is only the senses moving among the things of sense.

Whoever acts laying all his actions on Brahman, having let go of attachment, is untouched by evil — as a lotus leaf is untouched by the water. With the body, with the mind, with the understanding, even with the bare senses alone, the disciplined act, having let go of all clinging, for the cleansing of the self. The disciplined one, giving up the fruit of his action, comes to a peace that is rooted and lasting; the undisciplined, driven by desire, clinging to the fruit, are bound fast.

Renouncing all actions with his mind, the one who has mastered himself sits at ease, the ruler of a city with nine gates, neither acting nor causing any action. It is not the Lord of the world who creates men's sense of agency, or their actions, or the joining of action to its fruit; it is their own nature at work. The all-pervading Lord takes on no one's evil and no one's good. Wisdom is veiled by ignorance, and so the world is led astray. But for those in whom that ignorance of the self has been destroyed by knowledge, knowledge shines out like the sun and makes the highest manifest. Their understanding fixed on it, their very self become it, made steadfast in it, taking it for their one goal, they go where there is no returning, their faults washed away by knowledge.

The learned, those who truly see, look with the same eye on a brahmin rich in learning and humility, on a cow, on an elephant, on a dog, and on an outcaste who lives by eating dogs. Even here, in this life, those whose minds rest in this sameness have conquered the cycle of birth and death; for Brahman is without flaw and the same in all, and so they are established in Brahman. Let a person not be carried away with gladness at getting what he likes, nor sink into bitterness at meeting what he hates; with his understanding steady and unshaken, knowing Brahman, he stands firm in Brahman.

Unattached to the touch of the world outside, he finds the happiness that is within the self; joined by discipline to Brahman, he tastes a joy that does not run dry. For the delights that are born of contact with the senses are themselves the wombs of pain — they have a beginning and an end, Arjuna — and the wise take no joy in them. Whoever can stand fast, even here, even before he is freed of the body, against the surge of desire and anger — that person is disciplined, that person is happy. The one whose happiness is within, whose peace is within, whose light is within — that disciplined soul, having become Brahman, comes to the peace of Brahman, the great extinction. The seers come to that peace, their faults worn away, their doubts cut through, their selves under control, rejoicing in the good of all that lives.

For those who have torn themselves free of desire and anger, who have mastered their thought, who know the self, the peace of Brahman lies near, on every side. Shutting out the things of sense from his mind, fixing his gaze between the brows, drawing the breath that flows out and the breath that flows in to an even pace within the nostrils, the sage who has made the senses, the mind, and the understanding his own, who has set his whole aim on release, who has thrown off desire and fear and anger — that sage is already, here and now, set free forever. And he comes to my peace, knowing me for the one who receives all offering and all worship, the great Lord of all the worlds, the friend of every living thing.

Krishna said: The one who does the work he ought to do, without leaning on its fruit, is the true renouncer, the true disciplined soul — not the one who merely lights no sacrificial fire and lifts a hand to no task. What the world calls renunciation, Arjuna, you should know to be the very discipline of action, the yoga of work; for no one becomes a disciplined soul who has not first let go of every grasping intention. For the sage who is climbing toward this discipline, work is said to be the means; for the one who has already reached it, stillness is the means. When a person is no longer bound to the objects of sense, no longer bound to his own deeds, when he has let go of every grasping intention, then he is said to have arrived.

Let a man lift himself up by his own self, and never let himself sink down; for the self is the friend of the self, and the self is also its enemy. To the man who has mastered himself, his own self is a friend; but to the man who has not, his own self stands against him like an enemy. The self of one who has conquered himself and found his peace is gathered and steady, alike in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, in honor and disgrace. He is the disciplined soul, full and content with the wisdom he has realized, unshaken, his senses mastered, to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and a lump of gold are all one and the same. And he stands highest of all who holds the same even regard for friend and companion and enemy alike, for the indifferent stranger and the one who hates him, for the good and the wicked together.

Let the seeker of this discipline withdraw to a solitary place and keep at his practice, alone, his thoughts and his whole self held in check, wanting nothing, owning nothing. Let him set up a firm seat for himself in a clean spot, neither too high nor too low, with a cloth and a deerskin and the kusha grass laid one upon another. There, seated, holding his mind to a single point, his thoughts and the working of his senses reined in, let him take up the practice of meditation to make his heart pure. Let him hold his body, his head, and his neck straight and unmoving, his gaze steady, looking toward the tip of his own nose and not glancing about in any direction. Serene and unafraid, firm in his vow of chastity, his mind held in check, let him sit absorbed, his thought fixed on me, intent on me alone. So practicing always, his mind held in, the disciplined soul comes at last to the peace that is the highest of all, the peace that abides in me.

But this discipline is not for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who eats nothing at all; it is not for the one who sleeps too much, nor for the one who keeps himself always awake, Arjuna. For the one whose food and recreation are measured, whose efforts in all his work are measured, whose sleeping and waking are measured — for that man the discipline becomes the very thing that puts an end to his sorrow. When the mind, held under control, comes to rest in the self alone, free of all craving for any object whatsoever, then a person is called a disciplined soul.

As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the image given for the disciplined yogi, his mind held in check, deep in the practice of communion with the self. When the mind comes to rest, stilled by the practice of this discipline; when, looking on the self by the self, a person finds his contentment in the self alone; when he knows that boundless joy which lies beyond the senses and is grasped by the awakened reason, and, knowing it, never again strays from the truth of it; and when, having gained it, he counts no other gain greater than this, and, settled in it, is not shaken even by the heaviest grief — that, you should know, is what is meant by yoga, the loosing of every bond with sorrow. This discipline must be practiced with resolve and with a heart that does not lose heart.

Letting go, without exception, of every desire born of his own scheming, holding in his senses from every side by the power of his mind, let him little by little come to rest, his reason held firm, his mind settled in the self and turned toward nothing else. Wherever the restless and unsteady mind wanders off, let him rein it back from there and bring it under the control of the self alone. For the deepest happiness comes to the yogi whose mind is at peace, whose passion has been stilled, who is without fault and has become one with the eternal. So keeping himself always in this discipline, freed from every stain, the yogi reaches with ease the boundless happiness of touching the eternal. The one whose self is joined in this discipline, who looks on all things with an even eye, sees the self present in every creature, and every creature present in the self. The one who sees me everywhere, and sees all things in me — I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me. The yogi who, settled in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all creatures, lives in me, whatever his outward way of life. And the one who, taking his own self as the measure, looks on all things as he looks on himself, Arjuna — whether in pleasure or in pain — that one is held to be the highest yogi of all.

Arjuna said: This discipline you have spoken of, Krishna, this equal-mindedness — I cannot see how it can hold steady, for the mind is so restless. The mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, willful, unyielding; to hold it down seems to me as hard as holding down the wind.

Krishna said: Beyond doubt, strong-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to hold; and yet, Arjuna, it can be held — by steady practice and by dispassion. For the man who has no command of himself, this discipline is hard to reach, I agree; but the man who strives, and who keeps a hold on himself, can reach it by the right means.

Arjuna said: But what of the one who has faith, yet cannot master himself, whose mind wanders away from the discipline before he reaches its goal — what becomes of him, Krishna? Failing of both worlds, does he not simply break apart like a torn cloud and come to nothing, with no firm ground beneath him, lost on the road to the eternal? Clear away this doubt of mine entirely, Krishna; there is no one but you who can clear it.

Krishna said: Son of Pritha, no such man is lost, neither in this world nor in the world to come. For no one who does what is good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. The one who falls short in this discipline reaches the worlds that belong to those who have done right, and dwells there for unmeasured years; and then he is born again into the house of the pure and the prosperous. Or he may even be born into a family of yogis who are wise — though a birth like that is very hard to come by in this world. There he recovers the understanding he had built up in his former body, and from that point he strives once more toward perfection, Arjuna. For the very practice of his earlier life carries him onward, even against his will. Even the one who only longs to know this discipline rises beyond the bare word of the scriptures. And the yogi who strives with all his strength, washed clean of every fault, perfected through many births, comes at last to the highest goal. The yogi is greater than those who punish their bodies in penance, greater than the learned, greater than those who pour out works of ritual; so be a yogi, Arjuna. And of all yogis, the one I hold to be the most deeply joined to me is the one who worships me with faith, his inmost self resting in me.

Krishna said: Now hear, Arjuna, how with your mind fixed wholly on me, taking refuge in me and practicing this discipline, you will come to know me through and through, beyond all doubt. I will teach you this knowledge, and the deeper insight that goes with it, in full; once you have it, there is nothing more left to know in this world.
Of many thousands of people, scarcely one strives for perfection; and of those who strive and reach it, scarcely one truly knows me as I am.

Earth, water, fire, air, and ether; mind, intellect, and the sense of "I" — this is my nature, divided eightfold. But this is only my lower nature, Arjuna. Know that I have another, a higher nature: the very principle of life, by which this whole world is held up and sustained. All things that live are born of these two natures of mine. I am the origin of the whole universe, and its dissolution as well. There is nothing higher than I am; everything that exists is strung upon me like rows of pearls upon a single thread.

I am the taste in water, Arjuna; I am the light in the moon and the sun; I am the sacred syllable OM that sounds in all the Vedas, the sound in the air, the manhood in men. I am the pure scent of the earth and the brightness in fire; I am the life in all that lives, and the austerity of those who practice austerity. Know me, Arjuna, as the eternal seed of every living thing. I am the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendor of the splendid. I am the strength of the strong, free of desire and craving; and in all creatures I am desire itself, when that desire does not run against what is right.

Know, too, that the three qualities of nature — the lucid, the passionate, and the dark — all arise from me alone. They are in me, but I am not in them. Deluded by these three qualities, the whole world fails to recognize me, who stand beyond them, changeless. For this divine illusion of mine, this maya woven of the three qualities, is hard to see past; only those who take refuge in me alone pass beyond it.
Those who do evil do not turn to me — the deluded, the lowest of men, whose discernment has been stripped away by this same illusion, who have given themselves over to a demonic way of being.

Four kinds of good people turn to me in worship, Arjuna: the one in distress, the one who seeks knowledge, the one who seeks some good of his own, and the one who already knows. Of these, the one who knows — the wise one, ever steadfast, devoted to the one alone — stands highest; for I am dear above all things to the wise, and he is dear to me. All four are noble, but the wise one I hold to be my very self; for, steadied in this discipline, he has set his whole course on me, the highest goal there is. After many births the wise one comes at last to me, knowing that all this is the divine, that all this is God. Such a great soul is very hard to find.
