There are others whose discernment is carried off by this desire or that, and who turn instead to lesser gods, each according to his own nature, binding themselves with their various rites. But whatever form a devotee longs to worship in faith, it is I who steady that faith in him and make it firm. Held steady in that faith, he worships that god and gains from it the things he desires — though it is I, in truth, who grant them. Yet the reward such people win is limited and passing. Those who worship the gods go to the gods; but those who are devoted to me come to me.

Men of little understanding take me, the unmanifest, to be merely manifest — some particular form — not knowing my higher nature, which is changeless and beyond all compare. I am not revealed to everyone, veiled as I am by the illusion of my own power; this bewildered world does not recognize me, the unborn and the unchanging. I know all beings, Arjuna — those that are past, those that are present, and those that are yet to come; but no one knows me.

By the pull of the pairs of opposites, by the delusion that springs from craving and aversion, all creatures fall into confusion at their very birth. But those who do what is good, whose wrongdoing has come to an end, are freed from the delusion of these opposites; firm in their resolve, they worship me. Those who take refuge in me and strive for release from old age and death come to know Brahman entire — the whole self, and the whole of action. Those who know me as the ground of all that lives, the ground of all the gods, and the ground of all sacrifice — who know me with their minds held steady — they know me even in the hour of their death.

sections.label: Chapter VIII
sections.title: The Hour of Death and the Imperishable

segments.text: Arjuna said: Tell me, best of all, what is that Brahman? What is the Self, the adhyatma? What is action, karma? What do you call the realm of beings, the adhibhuta, and what the realm of the gods, the adhidaiva? Who, here in this body, is the lord of sacrifice, the adhiyajna — and how is he the lord of it? And at the hour of death, Krishna, how are you to be known by those who keep themselves in check?

Krishna said: Brahman is the supreme, the imperishable; the Self is what it is called as it dwells in each person. Action is the creative force that sends all beings forth and holds them in being. The realm of beings is my perishable nature; the realm of the gods is the spirit, the Purusha, who lies behind them; and the lord of sacrifice is I myself, here within this body, scourge of your enemies — for every offering is made to me.

And at the hour of death, the one who lets go of the body remembering me alone, and goes out so, comes into my being; of this there is no doubt. But whatever state a person dwells on as he leaves the body at the end, to that state he goes, Arjuna, having been shaped by it all his life long. So at all times remember me, and fight. With your mind and your understanding fixed on me, you will come to me; do not doubt it. The one whose thought is disciplined by constant practice, never straying after anything else, reaches the supreme spirit, the divine Purusha — for to meditate on him is to go to him.

Whoever holds in mind the ancient Seer, the ruler of all, smaller than the smallest, the sustainer of everything, whose form is past imagining, radiant as the sun and beyond all darkness — whoever holds him so at the hour of death, with a still mind and an unwavering devotion, the breath drawn up between the brows by the power of his discipline, that person reaches the supreme spirit, the divine Purusha.

I will tell you, in brief, of that imperishable goal which those who know the Vedas call the changeless, which the seekers enter once they are free of all craving, the goal for which they take up the discipline of chastity. The one who closes all the gates of the senses, who pens the mind up within the heart, who draws his life-breath up into the head and holds himself firm in the practice of his discipline, and who, uttering the single sacred syllable OM — the sound of Brahman — keeps me in mind as he goes out from the body: that person walks the highest road. To the one who thinks of me always, whose mind never turns aside to anything else, to that disciplined soul, ever steadfast, I am easy to reach. Having reached me, these great souls are not born again into this fleeting house of sorrow; they have come to the highest perfection.

All the worlds, Arjuna, up to the very world of Brahma the creator, are places of return: a soul that reaches them comes back again. But the one who reaches me is born no more. Those who understand that a day of Brahma lasts a thousand ages, and that his night also lasts a thousand ages — they are the ones who truly know what day and night are. When that long day dawns, all things come forth into the visible world out of the unmanifest; when that long night falls, they dissolve back again into the same unmanifest. This whole host of beings, the very same, comes into existence again and again, and is dissolved, helpless, at the fall of night, and rises up again, helpless, at the break of day. But beyond this unmanifest there is another, a higher unmanifest still, everlasting, which does not perish when all things perish. This unmanifest, this imperishable, is called the supreme goal; and those who reach it never return. That is my highest dwelling place. That supreme spirit, Arjuna, in whom all beings rest and by whom this whole universe is spread out, can be reached by a devotion that turns to nothing else.

Now I will tell you of the times at which those who are disciplined go out from the body never to return, and the times at which they go out only to come back. Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight of the waxing moon, the six months of the sun's northern journey — those who know Brahman and go out by this path go on to Brahman. Smoke, the night, the dark fortnight of the waning moon, the six months of the sun's southern journey — by this path the disciplined one reaches only the light of the moon, and returns. These two ways of the world, the bright and the dark, are held to be everlasting. By the one a soul goes and does not come back; by the other it goes and returns again. Knowing these two paths, Arjuna, no disciplined soul is ever deluded; so at all times hold fast to this discipline.

Whatever fruit of merit is promised in the Vedas, in the sacrifices, in penance, in the giving of gifts — the disciplined soul who has understood this teaching passes beyond all of it, and comes at last to the supreme, the first and highest dwelling place.

sections.label: Chapter IX
sections.title: The Royal Knowledge and the Royal Secret

segments.text: Krishna said: To you, who find no fault in it, I will now reveal this deepest knowledge, this most secret wisdom, knowing which you will be freed from all that is wrong. This is the royal knowledge, the royal secret, the purest of all; you can see its truth for yourself, it accords with what is right, it is easy to live by, and it never wears away.

Those who put no faith in this teaching, son of Bharata, do not reach me; they return again to the round of death and change. By me, in my unseen form, this whole universe is spread out. All beings rest in me, but I am not in them. And yet they do not rest in me either — look on this, the mystery of my power: my self gives birth to all beings and sustains them, and still it does not dwell within them. As the mighty wind moves everywhere, yet always remains within space, so all beings remain within me. Understand this.

At the end of an age, Arjuna, all beings return into the nature that is mine; at the beginning of the next, I send them forth again. Holding sway over the nature that is my own, again and again I send forth this whole host of beings, helpless as they are under the power of that nature. Yet these acts do not bind me, Arjuna; I sit apart from them, like one indifferent, unattached to all this work. Under my oversight, nature brings forth everything that moves and everything that stands still; this is how the world keeps turning.

The deluded despise me when I take a human form, blind to the higher nature that is mine, the lord of all that lives. Their hopes are empty, their deeds are empty, their knowledge is empty; they have given themselves over to the deluded, fiendish nature that misleads. But the great souls, the mahatmas, who have taken on the divine nature, worship me with a mind that does not wander, knowing me to be the imperishable source of all beings. Always glorifying me, striving with firm vows, bowing before me in love, they wait on me with unbroken devotion. Others again worship me with the offering of knowledge, as the one, or the many, or the all — turned toward me in my every face.

I am the rite; I am the sacrifice; I am the offering made to the dead; I am the healing herb; I am the sacred word; I am the clarified butter, the fire, and the offering poured into it. I am the father of this world, its mother, the one who sustains it, its grandfather; I am what is to be known, the purifier, the sacred sound OM; I am the Rig, the Sama, and the Yajur Veda. I am the goal, the upholder, the lord, the witness, the home, the refuge, the friend; I am the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the resting place, the imperishable seed. I give heat; I hold back the rain and I send it; I am deathlessness, and I am death; I am what is and what is not, Arjuna.

Those who follow the three Vedas, who drink the sacred soma and are cleansed of their sins, who worship me with sacrifices seeking to reach heaven — they win the holy world of Indra and taste in the sky the divine pleasures of the gods. But when they have enjoyed that vast world of heaven, their merit spent, they fall back into the world of mortals. So those who follow the letter of the three Vedas, longing for pleasures, gain only what comes and goes. But those who worship me alone, thinking of nothing else, always devoted — to them, who are ever steadfast, I bring all they need and guard what they have.

Even those who, with faith, worship other gods, worship me, Arjuna — though not in the right way; for I am the one who receives every sacrifice, and its lord. But they do not know me as I truly am, and so they fall. Those who are vowed to the gods go to the gods; those vowed to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; but those who worship me come to me.

Whoever offers me, with love, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of love, made by the pure of heart, I gladly accept. So, Arjuna, whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, whatever discipline you take on, do it as an offering to me. In this way you will be freed from the bonds of action, from its good and evil fruit alike; with your mind made one with me through this discipline of renunciation, set free, you will come to me.

I am the same to all beings; none is hateful to me and none is dear. But those who worship me with love are in me, and I am in them. Even if the worst of sinners worships me, turning to me with his whole heart, he is to be counted among the good, for he has set his mind on the right path. Soon he becomes a soul devoted to what is right, and comes to lasting peace. Know this for certain, Arjuna: no one who is devoted to me is ever lost. For whoever takes refuge in me, son of Pritha — even those born of the womb of sin, women, vaishyas, and shudras too — reaches the highest. How much more, then, the holy brahmins and the devoted royal sages! So, since you have come into this fleeting world of sorrow, worship me. Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down before me; so, having made me your highest aim, your whole self joined to me, you shall come to me.
